questions.q: A sign of a cold solder joint:
options: A thin even layer of solder over the pad
questions.explain: The solder did not wet one of the sides; the joint breaks from vibration.

questions.q: Why tin both the wire and the pad before joining?
options: So that both sides are wetted
So as not to overheat the board and the pad
questions.explain: Tinned surfaces join in 1–2 s without overheating.

questions.q: Where do you secure a wire with a cable tie?
options: Right next to the joint, for stiffness
questions.explain: A stiff point next to another stiff point breaks the strands at the boundary.

questions.q: Why must you not strip insulation with a knife?
options: The knife gets dull on the copper strands
questions.explain: A stripper set to the gauge does not damage the strands.

questions.q: Which flux is unacceptable on electronics?
questions.explain: Active flux corrodes traces and wires.

questions.q: How do you check a power joint under load?
options: With a multimeter continuity check for an open circuit
questions.explain: A bad connection heats up under current (after a flight or under a 20–30 A bench load): a thermal camera or, carefully, a finger.

questions.q: Tip temperature for Sn63/Pb37 leaded solder:
questions.explain: The solder melts at 183 °C; the tip is held at 330–370 °C to heat the joint quickly.

questions.q: Why is the tinned section of a wire not made longer than the pad?
options: Otherwise the wire conducts current worse
It becomes stiff and breaks at the edge
questions.explain: An extra tinned section loses flexibility; the wire breaks at the boundary with the flexible part.
